description: Astronomers have noticed that a cluster of distant Kuiper Belt objects (icy bodies beyond Neptune) have oddly, and I mean oddly aligned orbits, which is best explained if there's a large undiscovered planet way out in the outer solar system: nicknamed "Planet X". It's never been directly seen. Let's possibly detect and visualize it in this hackathon, we might even discover more from this space hysteric glamour.
summary: Vestigium is a free website that lets anyone watch the sky move in real NASA SPHEREx pictures and test predictions against them. Visitors flip between pictures of the same patch of sky taken months or years apart, the method astronomers use to hunt for a hidden "Planet X", and see for example Barnard's Star move about 168 arcseconds in 16 years. It covers the five challenge targets plus Pluto, Makemake and comet 3I/ATLAS, with the date, wavelength and source on every picture. From our own measurements we forecast where Pluto would appear, locked the forecast in a public GitHub commit, and only then opened SPHEREx's newest Pluto pictures. Pluto was 5.9 arcseconds off: over 3,000 times closer than a straight-line guess, but just outside our 95% oval. We published it as a miss, found why, and locked new forecasts for 2027. We also measured whether SPHEREx could see Planet X by hiding 40,066 artificial planets in real pictures: for the nominal Planet Nine, one image is 4 to 7 magnitudes too shallow. It matters because it turns SPHEREx data into a hands-on lesson in how science works: predict, check, and report honestly, misses included.
details:
Code and data: https://github.com/Nama2323/tenger

Live site: https://nama2323.github.io/tenger/

WHAT IT DOES

Vestigium lets anyone watch the sky move in real NASA SPHEREx pictures, then test predictions against new observations, honestly.

- See: real SPHEREx images (data releases DR1 and QR3) of the five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), plus Pluto, Makemake and comet 3I/ATLAS. Visitors flip between dates with Blink, Swipe or Side by side, adjust contrast, and see the date, wavelength and source on every picture. A difference image appears only when two pictures truly match. An older AllWISE picture (about 2010) shows years of motion: Barnard's Star moved about 168 arcseconds in 16 years.

- Not scored (frozen as "too little data" in each trial file): WISE 0855 (no usable training positions), RW Aurigae (15 brightness measurements, but no regular pattern to forecast from), R Draconis (no usable training measurements), Makemake (no usable detections). Comet 3I/ATLAS is shown only, with no forecast.
- 3D map: a live 3D Solar System with our targets in their real sky directions. Planets follow JPL's orbits; a time control runs from 1900 to 2050, and visitors can fly to any planet.

- Predict and check: we forecast where a target will appear in the newest SPHEREx pictures, lock the forecast in a public GitHub commit before anyone opens those pictures, then score it with a fixed rule (inside the 95% region is a hit). Every result is published, misses included. A step-by-step reveal shows the Pluto test, with a zoomed view of the miss.

- Planet X: we measured whether SPHEREx could see Planet Nine by hiding artificial planets in real images, and a "Find the hidden planet" game uses those clearly labelled artificial planets.

- Learn and play: "Beat the physics" lets visitors guess where a star or Pluto goes next (Easy mode shows the direction and a date ruler, worked out only from the dots on screen), compare with a straight line and our physics, and send a "Challenge a friend" link (no account, no stored data). Three printable lessons for grades 8 to 11 cover distance from motion, comparing brightness, and how sure a forecast can be.

OUR RESULTS

- Pluto (blind test: forecast locked before the newest pictures were opened): a miss. Pluto was 5.90 arcseconds from our forecast, just outside our 95% region; a straight-line guess was 5.5 degrees off, over 3,000 times worse. We did find Pluto: our position is 0.35 arcseconds from JPL Horizons. Cause: our 50 training detections were really 6 linked groups, so our error region was too small.
